This produces your application and the rule that decides the amount. It does not calculate the amount. The figure comes from a table that takes an income defined by O. Reg. 391/97 s. 16 and adjusted by Schedule III, and ss. 17 to 20 let a court determine that income differently again. Nothing on this site works out what you would receive or owe.

QUESTION 1

Who is applying, and who is the application against?

QUESTION 2

Where does the other parent ordinarily live?

This decides which table applies, so it is worth getting right. O. Reg. 391/97 s. 2 (1) selects the table for the province or territory where the parent the order is sought againstordinarily resides — not where the children live and not where the case is filed. If they live elsewhere in Canada, that province’s or territory’s table applies. If they live outside Canada, or you do not know where they live, the Ontario table applies when you live in Ontario (s. 2 (1), “table”, (b) and (e)).

QUESTION 3

Tell me about the children this is for.

Each child’s age, and what each is doing now — at school, working, or something else. In your own words; this goes into the application as you write it.

QUESTION 4

How is the children’s time divided between you at the moment?

Recorded as you describe it. Whether O. Reg. 391/97 s. 8 or s. 9 applies to an arrangement is for the court; nothing here decides that.

QUESTION 5

What is the other parent’s annual income, and where does that figure come from?

Write it however you know it. If you are unsure, say so in your own words — “about $60,000” is recorded as you wrote it and is not rounded or changed.

We have both agreed on this figure, in writing.
O. Reg. 391/97 s. 15 (2) provides that where both parties agree in writing on the annual income of a party, the court may consider that amount to be their income if it thinks the amount is reasonable having regard to the income information provided under s. 21. A figure agreed in writing and a figure one person states are read differently, so the application says which this is.
When a court works out the income figure itself
s. 17 — Where the court is of the opinion that s. 16 would not be the fairest determination, it may have regard to income over the last three years and determine an amount that is fair and reasonable in light of any pattern, fluctuation, or non-recurring amount.
s. 18 — Where a person is a shareholder, director or officer of a corporation and the court is of the opinion that s. 16 does not fairly reflect all the money available for support, the court may include corporate pre-tax income or an amount commensurate with services provided.
s. 19 — The court may impute income in circumstances the section lists, including intentional under-employment or unemployment, diverted income, property not reasonably used to generate income, failure to provide income information when legally obliged to, and unreasonably deducted expenses.
s. 20 — Where a person is a non-resident, income is generally determined as though they were a resident of Canada, with a different rule where they reside where effective tax rates are significantly higher.
Schedule III, item 9 — Salaries, benefits, wages or management fees paid to non-arm's-length persons and deducted from net self-employment income are added back UNLESS the person establishes the payments were necessary to earn the income and reasonable in the circumstances. That is something a person must establish, not something to be calculated.
Schedule III, item 12 — Where income is earned through a partnership or sole proprietorship, an amount included in income that is "properly required" by the business for capitalization is deducted. Whether an amount is properly required is a judgment, not arithmetic.

QUESTION 6

Is this only about the table amount for the children?

If it is — no spousal support, no share of special expenses, nothing about property — Family Law Rules r. 13 (1.3) means you do not have to file a financial statement at all. That is a whole form you would otherwise complete.

Yes, only the table amount

Which income documents do you already have? One per line.

HOW THE TABLE WORKS

How a table amount is worked out: find the income row, then add the percentage

This explains how the table is built. It is not about your case, and no amount is worked out here or anywhere else on this site.

Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 3 (1)

Unless otherwise provided under these guidelines, the amount of an order for the support of a child for children under the age of majority is,

(a) the amount set out in the applicable table, according to the number of children under the age of majority to whom the order relates and the income of the parent or spouse against whom the order is sought; and

(b) the amount, if any, determined under section 7.

Two parts, and only the first comes from the table. Section 7 covers special or extraordinary expenses, and the court decides those separately.

Which table — it depends on where the other parent lives

Ontario does not publish a table of its own. O. Reg. 303/24 revoked the one it had, and s. 2 (1) of the Ontario Guidelines now defines “table” by pointing at the federal tables:

“table” means,

(a) if the parent or spouse against whom an order is sought ordinarily resides in Ontario at the time of the application, the table set out in the Federal Child Support Guidelines for Ontario,

(b) if the parent or spouse against whom an order is sought ordinarily resides elsewhere in Canada, the table set out in the Federal Child Support Guidelines for the province or territory in which the parent or spouse ordinarily resides at the time of the application …

It is where the person the order is sought againstordinarily resides — not where the case is filed and not where the child lives. Your own residence matters only if that person lives outside Canada or where they live is unknown: then the Ontario table applies when you live in Ontario (paragraph (e)). Paragraphs (c) and (d) go further: a court may use a different province’s table where that residence has changed since the application, or will change in the near future.

What a table looks like

Each table is headed by a province and a number of children, and carries two tiers of columns. The columns below are shown empty on purpose — the figures are at the source.

Income ($)	Monthly Award ($)
From	To	Basic Amount	Plus (%)	Of Income Over
—	—	—	—	—

A row’s award is not the Basic Amount on its own. It is the Basic Amount plusthe percentage in Plus (%) applied to the income above the “Of Income Over” figure, which is the floor of that row’s band. That is what makes a row a calculation rather than an answer.

The income the table takes is a defined figure

It is not a salary and not a take-home figure. O. Reg. 391/97 s. 16 determines annual income using the sources listed under “Total income” in the T1 General form, adjusted in accordance with Schedule III. Sections 17 to 20 set out circumstances in which a court determines the figure differently again — a pattern of income over three years, income from a corporation, or an amount imputed to a parent or spouse.

That is why this site records what you tell it about income and does not turn it into a support amount. The figure the table takes is one a court determines.

Sources, read in full at: O. Reg. 391/97 (Ontario) · SOR/97-175 (federal) · the federal tables themselves. Verified 2026-09-15.

There is a support order but the payments are not being made — who enforces it?

Where things stand

Ontario has a Director of the Family Responsibility Office. The Director's job is to enforce support orders filed in the Director's office. This applies when the order, and any support deduction order that goes with it, are filed there. The Director pays what is collected to the person it is owed to. The clerk or registrar of the court that made a support order must file it there promptly once it is signed.

What to do next

While a support order is filed there, only the Director may enforce it. The one exception is someone given the Director's powers under section 4 of the Act. The Director may refuse to enforce all or part of a filed order in some cases the Act lists. They include an order whose meaning is unclear. They also include when the person owed support has not met reasonable requests for facts the Director needs. An order that was withdrawn from the Director's office may be filed there again at any time. The payor or the recipient does this by signing a written notice. A support order and any support deduction order that goes with it must be filed again together. Whoever files or refiles a support order there must give notice right away. It goes to the clerk at any court office where the recipient is enforcing the order. It can be sent by mail or email. It can also be sent online, through Justice Services Online or the Ontario Courts Public Portal, whichever is available. A person owed support who files the order there may have started to enforce it on their own. If the Director asks, they must hand that over to the Director. A payment order is a temporary or final order to pay money to another person, such as a support order. It does not include a provisional order. The Family Law Rules list ways to enforce a payment order. Who uses these ways depends on where the order is. While a support order is filed in the Director's office, only the Director may use them, apart from the exception above. If it is not filed there, the person owed the money may. The ways include a request for a financial statement, seizure and sale, and garnishment. A default hearing can also be used if the order is a support order. When the Director enforces an order, the rules for the person the order favours apply to the Director. Other orders may be enforced in three ways. They are a writ to seize property for a time, a contempt order, and naming a receiver. All of these are in addition to other ways the law provides.

What happens after

Using one way to enforce a support order does not stop other ways at the same time or at other times. The Director may enforce arrears that built up before the order was filed there. Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 3 (1)

Unless otherwise provided under these guidelines, the amount of an order for the support of a child for children under the age of majority is,

(a) the amount set out in the applicable table, according to the number of children under the age of majority to whom the order relates and the income of the parent or spouse against whom the order is sought; and

(b) the amount, if any, determined under section 7.

Two parts, and only the first comes from the table. Section 7 covers special or extraordinary expenses, and the court decides those separately.

Which table — it depends on where the other parent lives

Ontario does not publish a table of its own. O. Reg. 303/24 revoked the one it had, and s. 2 (1) of the Ontario Guidelines now defines “table” by pointing at the federal tables:

“table” means,

(a) if the parent or spouse against whom an order is sought ordinarily resides in Ontario at the time of the application, the table set out in the Federal Child Support Guidelines for Ontario,

(b) if the parent or spouse against whom an order is sought ordinarily resides elsewhere in Canada, the table set out in the Federal Child Support Guidelines for the province or territory in which the parent or spouse ordinarily resides at the time of the application …

It is where the person the order is sought againstordinarily resides — not where the case is filed and not where the child lives. Your own residence matters only if that person lives outside Canada or where they live is unknown: then the Ontario table applies when you live in Ontario (paragraph (e)). Paragraphs (c) and (d) go further: a court may use a different province’s table where that residence has changed since the application, or will change in the near future.

What a table looks like

Each table is headed by a province and a number of children, and carries two tiers of columns. The columns below are shown empty on purpose — the figures are at the source.

Income ($)	Monthly Award ($)
From	To	Basic Amount	Plus (%)	Of Income Over
—	—	—	—	—

A row’s award is not the Basic Amount on its own. It is the Basic Amount plusthe percentage in Plus (%) applied to the income above the “Of Income Over” figure, which is the floor of that row’s band. That is what makes a row a calculation rather than an answer.

The income the table takes is a defined figure

It is not a salary and not a take-home figure. O. Reg. 391/97 s. 16 determines annual income using the sources listed under “Total income” in the T1 General form, adjusted in accordance with Schedule III. Sections 17 to 20 set out circumstances in which a court determines the figure differently again — a pattern of income over three years, income from a corporation, or an amount imputed to a parent or spouse.

That is why this site records what you tell it about income and does not turn it into a support amount. The figure the table takes is one a court determines.

There is a support order but the payments are not being made — who enforces it?

Where things stand

Ontario has a Director of the Family Responsibility Office. The Director's job is to enforce support orders filed in the Director's office. This applies when the order, and any support deduction order that goes with it, are filed there. The Director pays what is collected to the person it is owed to. The clerk or registrar of the court that made a support order must file it there promptly once it is signed.

What to do next

While a support order is filed there, only the Director may enforce it. The one exception is someone given the Director's powers under section 4 of the Act. The Director may refuse to enforce all or part of a filed order in some cases the Act lists. They include an order whose meaning is unclear. They also include when the person owed support has not met reasonable requests for facts the Director needs. An order that was withdrawn from the Director's office may be filed there again at any time. The payor or the recipient does this by signing a written notice. A support order and any support deduction order that goes with it must be filed again together. Whoever files or refiles a support order there must give notice right away. It goes to the clerk at any court office where the recipient is enforcing the order. It can be sent by mail or email. It can also be sent online, through Justice Services Online or the Ontario Courts Public Portal, whichever is available. A person owed support who files the order there may have started to enforce it on their own. If the Director asks, they must hand that over to the Director. A payment order is a temporary or final order to pay money to another person, such as a support order. It does not include a provisional order. The Family Law Rules list ways to enforce a payment order. Who uses these ways depends on where the order is. While a support order is filed in the Director's office, only the Director may use them, apart from the exception above. If it is not filed there, the person owed the money may. The ways include a request for a financial statement, seizure and sale, and garnishment. A default hearing can also be used if the order is a support order. When the Director enforces an order, the rules for the person the order favours apply to the Director. Other orders may be enforced in three ways. They are a writ to seize property for a time, a contempt order, and naming a receiver. All of these are in addition to other ways the law provides.

What happens after

Using one way to enforce a support order does not stop other ways at the same time or at other times. The Director may enforce arrears that built up before the order was filed there. If an order is withdrawn, the Director must stop enforcing it. But the Director may keep enforcing to collect arrears owed to an agency from a past assignment.

There is a support order but the payments are not being made — who enforces it?

Where things stand

Ontario has a Director of the Family Responsibility Office. The Director's job is to enforce support orders filed in the Director's office. This applies when the order, and any support deduction order that goes with it, are filed there. The Director pays what is collected to the person it is owed to. The clerk or registrar of the court that made a support order must file it there promptly once it is signed.

What to do next

While a support order is filed there, only the Director may enforce it. The one exception is someone given the Director's powers under section 4 of the Act. The Director may refuse to enforce all or part of a filed order in some cases the Act lists. They include an order whose meaning is unclear. They also include when the person owed support has not met reasonable requests for facts the Director needs. An order that was withdrawn from the Director's office may be filed there again at any time. The payor or the recipient does this by signing a written notice. A support order and any support deduction order that goes with it must be filed again together. Whoever files or refiles a support order there must give notice right away. It goes to the clerk at any court office where the recipient is enforcing the order. It can be sent by mail or email. It can also be sent online, through Justice Services Online or the Ontario Courts Public Portal, whichever is available. A person owed support who files the order there may have started to enforce it on their own. If the Director asks, they must hand that over to the Director. A payment order is a temporary or final order to pay money to another person, such as a support order. It does not include a provisional order. The Family Law Rules list ways to enforce a payment order. Who uses these ways depends on where the order is. While a support order is filed in the Director's office, only the Director may use them, apart from the exception above. If it is not filed there, the person owed the money may. The ways include a request for a financial statement, seizure and sale, and garnishment. A default hearing can also be used if the order is a support order. When the Director enforces an order, the rules for the person the order favours apply to the Director. Other orders may be enforced in three ways. They are a writ to seize property for a time, a contempt order, and naming a receiver. All of these are in addition to other ways the law provides.

What happens after

Using one way to enforce a support order does not stop other ways at the same time or at other times. The Director may enforce arrears that built up before the order was filed there. If an order is withdrawn, the Director must stop enforcing it. But the Director may keep enforcing to collect arrears owed to an agency from a past assignment.

Support if family violence is part of your situation
Who to contact, and how

If family violence is part of what you're dealing with, Ontario has support services separate from the court process itself. A Family Court Support Worker can help you understand and go through the family court process if you're a victim of domestic violence -- Family Court Support Workers do not give legal advice, but they can help you understand what's happening and connect you to other services. Every courthouse also has a Family Law Information Centre (FLIC) that provides information about the court process and referrals to local resources.

Ontario also names specific support organizations for family violence:
- Assaulted Women's Helpline: 1-866-863-0511 (toll-free), or 416-863-0511
- Fem'aide (French-language support): 1-877-336-2433 (toll-free)
- Victim Support Line: 1-888-579-2888 (toll-free), or 416-314-2447

The Family Court Support Worker Program and the Family Law Information Centre are delivered locally through each court location rather than through a single province-wide phone number. To find the Family Court Support Worker for your court, use Ontario's own listing of service providers by court location, which links directly to the organization delivering the program there. To reach the Family Law Information Centre, contact or visit the courthouse handling your case -- Ontario's own courthouse listing gives the address and contact information, including a phone number, for each location.

There is a support order but the payments are not being made — who enforces it?

Where things stand

Ontario has a Director of the Family Responsibility Office. The Director's job is to enforce support orders filed in the Director's office. This applies when the order, and any support deduction order that goes with it, are filed there. The Director pays what is collected to the person it is owed to. The clerk or registrar of the court that made a support order must file it there promptly once it is signed.

What to do next

While a support order is filed there, only the Director may enforce it. The one exception is someone given the Director's powers under section 4 of the Act. The Director may refuse to enforce all or part of a filed order in some cases the Act lists. They include an order whose meaning is unclear. They also include when the person owed support has not met reasonable requests for facts the Director needs. An order that was withdrawn from the Director's office may be filed there again at any time. The payor or the recipient does this by signing a written notice. A support order and any support deduction order that goes with it must be filed again together. Whoever files or refiles a support order there must give notice right away. It goes to the clerk at any court office where the recipient is enforcing the order. It can be sent by mail or email. It can also be sent online, through Justice Services Online or the Ontario Courts Public Portal, whichever is available. A person owed support who files the order there may have started to enforce it on their own. If the Director asks, they must hand that over to the Director. A payment order is a temporary or final order to pay money to another person, such as a support order. It does not include a provisional order. The Family Law Rules list ways to enforce a payment order. Who uses these ways depends on where the order is. While a support order is filed in the Director's office, only the Director may use them, apart from the exception above. If it is not filed there, the person owed the money may. The ways include a request for a financial statement, seizure and sale, and garnishment. A default hearing can also be used if the order is a support order. When the Director enforces an order, the rules for the person the order favours apply to the Director. Other orders may be enforced in three ways. They are a writ to seize property for a time, a contempt order, and naming a receiver. All of these are in addition to other ways the law provides.

What happens after

Using one way to enforce a support order does not stop other ways at the same time or at other times. The Director may enforce arrears that built up before the order was filed there. If an order is withdrawn, the Director must stop enforcing it. But the Director may keep enforcing to collect arrears owed to an agency from a past assignment.

Support if family violence is part of your situation
Who to contact, and how

If family violence is part of what you're dealing with, Ontario has support services separate from the court process itself. A Family Court Support Worker can help you understand and go through the family court process if you're a victim of domestic violence -- Family Court Support Workers do not give legal advice, but they can help you understand what's happening and connect you to other services. Every courthouse also has a Family Law Information Centre (FLIC) that provides information about the court process and referrals to local resources.

Ontario also names specific support organizations for family violence:
- Assaulted Women's Helpline: 1-866-863-0511 (toll-free), or 416-863-0511
- Fem'aide (French-language support): 1-877-336-2433 (toll-free)
- Victim Support Line: 1-888-579-2888 (toll-free), or 416-314-2447

The Family Court Support Worker Program and the Family Law Information Centre are delivered locally through each court location rather than through a single province-wide phone number. To find the Family Court Support Worker for your court, use Ontario's own listing of service providers by court location, which links directly to the organization delivering the program there. To reach the Family Law Information Centre, contact or visit the courthouse handling your case -- Ontario's own courthouse listing gives the address and contact information, including a phone number, for each location.
